newsitem.title: UK: Major comes out fighting, but no election date.
newsitem.headline: Major comes out fighting, but no election date.

text.p: With speculation mounting over the date of an approaching general election, British Prime Minister John Major accused the opposition Labour Party on Thursday of gesture politics by using the crisis over "mad cow" disease to try to bring down his government.

Amid speculation in parliament that Major, whose Conservatives lag badly in opinion polls, may announce a snap election in a speech on Friday, Major declined to give a hint on the timing of a poll that must be held by May 22.

Labour on Monday will move a motion in parliament to reduce the salary of Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, effectively a demand for the resignation of the man who has piloted Britain's attempts to have a European Union ban on beef exports lifted.

A successful vote is seen as a remote possibility. Although Major lacks an overall parliamentary majority, for Labour to win Monday's vote it would need strong backing from minority parties in the House of Commons.
Should it happen, however, there could be a confidence vote the following day and defeat for Major in this would force an election.
Major could pre-empt this process by announcing an early election -- on March 20 -- when he speaks to the annual conference of the Welsh Conservative Party on Friday (eds:1300 gmt).
In parliament on Thursday, Major accused Labour leader Tony Blair of persistently using the crisis over mad cow disease for his own political ends.

"Not once has he put the interests of the British beef industry ahead of making party political points," Major said. "Before he does more damage to the British beef industry, he should reflect on the damage he has already done."

British beef exports have been banned by the European Union since last March when the government admitted people could contract the human form of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy by eating infected beef. Major returned from a EU summit in Florence in June promising there would progress on lifting the ban by November. Despite this, it has remained in place.

Blair said the government's handling of the crisis, which has cost 3.3 billion pounds ($5.39 billion) and led to the slaughter of thousands of cattle, was a "symbol of incompetence in the most incompetent government in living memory".
Major held a 1-1/2 hour meeting of his cabinet before he appeared in parliament, but aides did not respond to questions about whether the timing of the election was discussed.
Asked about this in parliament by Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, Major parried the question, trumpeting the economic achievements of his government.
Major does not have to hold an election until May 22, and with his party almost 20 points behind Labour in the polls, he has been reluctant to contemplate an early contest.

However, an advantage of a March general election is that it could mean a February 27 parliamentary by-election in North-West England, which the Conservatives look set to lose ignominiously, would not take place.
For Labour to win Monday's vote, it would have to have need strong backing from minority parties in the House of Commons.

But Martyn Smith, a member of the nine-strong Ulster Unionist Party , said on Thursday that he would be in Northern Ireland for a constituency meeting, and at least one of his colleagues was also likely to be absent.

"It would be very foolish to come for a bogus vote in the House and miss the opportunity of meeting my supporters," he told independent television. Major's party and the combined opposition have 322 MPs each in parliament.
